extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning introductory set theory and basic logic
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory textbook material and exercises covering basic set theory (subset, power set, union/intersection/difference, complement, indexed sets, Venn diagrams) and an introduction to logic. Includes definitions, facts, illustrative examples, and exercises for practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying subsets (informal criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises like this help you identify what is and isn't a subset. You know immediately that a set such as {1,3} is not a subset of B because it can't be made by selecting elements from B, as the 3 is not an element of B and thus is not a valid selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the idea of 'selecting elements from B' to determine subset membership. Check whether every element of the candidate subset actually belongs to the larger set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish element versus subset
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples illustrate that an object can be an element of a set (x ∈ A) or a set itself that may be an element or subset (e.g. 1 ∈ {1,{1}}; {1} is the second element listed in {1,{1}}; {1} ⊆ {1,{1}} by selecting 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully parse nesting: a bare object (like 1) vs its singleton {1} behave differently. Verify whether the statement is about membership (∈) or subset relation (⊆).

rubrics_metrics.name: Power set (Definition 1.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a set, the power set of A is another set, denoted P(A) and defined to be the set of all subsets of A. In symbols, P(A) = {X : X ⊆ A}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For finite A list all subsets explicitly (example: P({1,2,3}) = {∅,{1},{2},{3},{1,2},{1,3},{2,3},{1,2,3}}). For infinite A, P(A) is too large to list; reason about its nature instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinality of power set for finite sets (Fact 1.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a finite set, then |P(A)| = 2^{|A|}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this fact to compute the number of subsets of a finite set. Example checks in the text confirm the 2^n formula in specific cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of power sets of infinite sets
rubrics_metrics.description: For infinite sets (e.g., N or R^2) the power set contains infinitely many and vastly many types of subsets — e.g., points, graphs of functions, black-and-white images, even the full text of every book — making P(R^2) 'mind boggling.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to list P(A) when A is infinite; instead reason about types of subsets and cardinality properties where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union, intersection, difference (Definition 1.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose A and B are sets. The union A ∪ B = {x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B}. The intersection A ∩ B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B}. The difference A - B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret in words: union = in A or B (or both); intersection = in both; difference = in A but not in B. Use set-builder notation and examples to check understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic algebraic properties of union/intersection/difference
rubrics_metrics.description: For any sets X and Y it is always true that X ∪ Y = Y ∪ X and X ∩ Y = Y ∩ X, but in general X - Y ≠ Y - X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use commutativity of ∪ and ∩ when simplifying expressions. Remember difference is not symmetric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartesian product interactions with set operations (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples show how Cartesian product interacts with intersections/unions: e.g., (A ∩ B) × B equals the listed ordered pairs in the example; (A × C) ∩ (B × C) = (A ∩ B) × C in the worked examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dealing with products, reason coordinatewise: membership in a product requires membership in each factor; intersection of products often factors as product of intersections when the second factor is the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interval examples for union/intersection/difference
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch intervals on the number line to visualize unions/intersections/differences; use endpoint conventions (closed/open) carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complement (Definition 1.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let A be a set with a universal set U. The complement of A, denoted A^c (or A with overbar), is the set A^c = U - A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always specify or understand the ambient universal set U when talking about complements. Example: primes P in N have complement N - P = {1,4,6,8,...}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venn diagrams as a reasoning tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent sets with circles/ovals in a universal set to illustrate combinations via shading. Venn diagrams are useful 'scratch work' for understanding how sets combine and for developing proof strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Venn diagrams to visualize unions, intersections, differences, and to check equality/containment relations; they are informal aids rather than formal proof, but help form correct set expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses rules for expressions with ∪ and ∩ (Important Points)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an expression involving sets uses only ∪, then parentheses are optional. If an expression uses only ∩, then parentheses are optional. If an expression uses both ∪ and ∩, then parentheses are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because ∪ and ∩ are associative among themselves, you may drop parentheses when only one operation appears; when mixed, keep parentheses to avoid ambiguity (e.g., (A ∪ B) ∩ C vs A ∪ (B ∩ C)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexed sets and big-union/big-intersection notation (Definition 1.7 / 1.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given sets A1, A2, ..., An, the union ⋃_{i=1}^n A_i = {x : x ∈ A_i for at least one i}; the intersection ⋂_{i=1}^n A_i = {x : x ∈ A_i for every i}. For collections indexed by a set I use ⋃_{a∈I} A_a and ⋂_{a∈I} A_a. The index set I need not consist of integers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the big-union/big-intersection notation to compactly express unions/intersections of many (possibly infinite) sets. Be comfortable with arbitrary index sets (letters, real numbers, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric example of indexed unions
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: For a ∈ [0,2], define A_a = {[1,2] × {a}} (horizontal segments). Then ⋃_{a∈[0,2]} A_a = [1,2] × [0,2] while ⋂_{a∈[0,2]} A_a = ∅.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualize indexed collections of sets as families; unions can 'fill in' regions (e.g., a rectangle), intersections may be empty even if each set is nonempty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-ordering principle for N
rubrics_metrics.description: Any non-empty subset of N has a smallest element (the well-ordering principle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this intuitive fact frequently in proofs about integers (often without explicit mention). It underlies proofs such as the division algorithm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division Algorithm (Fact 1.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given integers a and b with b > 0, there exist integers q and r for which a = q b + r and 0 < r < b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fact (derivable from the well-ordering principle) guarantees existence of quotient and remainder; apply it when dividing integers. (Note: the text states 0 < r < b in the worked derivation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Russell's paradox and the need for axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Russell's paradox arises from the 'set of all sets that are not elements of themselves' and the question 'Is A an element of A?'. The paradox motivated a careful examination of set theory leading to axioms (Zermelo-Fraenkel) including the axiom of foundation, which forbids circularly defined sets like X = {X}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that naive comprehension (forming arbitrary sets by property) can lead to contradictions; formal axiomatic set theory (ZF) resolves these by restricting allowable set constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic: distinction between correct logic and correct information
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is a process of deducing information correctly, not just deducing correct information. An argument can be logically valid (correctly combining premises) even if some premises are false; correctness of premises is separate from correctness of the deductive process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In proofs, aim for both valid logical steps and true premises; nonetheless, analyzing consequences of false assumptions can be useful and is legitimate logical reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a statement (start of Logic chapter)
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement is a sentence or mathematical expression that is either definitely true or definitely false — a piece of information to which logic can be applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate statements from non-statements (questions, commands, ambiguous expressions). Use statements as the basic units when applying formal logical rules.
